incident: The host times out connecting to huggingface.co on port 443, so config.json and weights cannot be downloaded. Other local applications are healthy.

The model Hub connection is reset on every download attempt, while a domestic mirror is reachable and the intended revision is known.
An offline inference node has no cached model artifact and cannot reach the remote repository. The service configuration itself is valid.

The trainer loads correctly, then OOMs only after increasing per-device train batch size. Sequence length and package versions are unchanged.

vllm bench crashes because datasets expects pyarrow.PyExtensionType, which was removed by the installed PyArrow release.
Installing an unrelated package upgraded transformers beyond the range required by the serving stack; imports now fail before CUDA initialization.
pip reports incompatible requirements for tokenizers and transformers, and the benchmark CLI fails during module import.
The environment contains packages from two experiments with mutually incompatible pydantic versions. A clean lockfile installation works elsewhere.
A partial package upgrade leaves vLLM and its benchmark extras on incompatible versions, producing an AttributeError at startup.
Downloading model shards stops with No space left on device. GPU memory is unused and the network remains connected.
The Hugging Face cache partition is 100% full and cannot write a temporary safetensors shard.
Checkpoint saving fails with errno 28 after training, although RAM and VRAM have free capacity.
The root filesystem has only a few megabytes free, and model extraction fails while a larger mounted volume is available.
A repeated experiment fills the cache with old snapshots, preventing the current model manifest from being written.
torch.cuda.is_available is false and PyTorch says the installed NVIDIA driver is too old for the CUDA runtime bundled in the wheel.
Importing a CUDA extension fails with an undefined CUDA symbol after upgrading torch without changing the host driver.
nvidia-smi works, but the application reports that its CUDA runtime version is unsupported by the current driver branch.
A newly installed cu130 torch wheel cannot initialize CUDA on a machine whose driver supports only an older runtime. Model files are local and valid.
The custom operator was compiled against a different CUDA major version than the active PyTorch build and fails to load its shared library.
The vLLM engine rejects new 8K requests because no KV cache blocks are available at concurrency 16. Model weights remain loaded and short requests still finish.
Long-context traffic fills every GPU KV block; requests wait indefinitely while GPU model memory is otherwise stable. Lower concurrency avoids the issue.
Startup reports enough room for only four 8192-token sequences, but the load test admits eight near-maximum prompts and stalls on cache allocation.
Decode scheduling repeatedly preempts long requests because the KV cache has no free blocks. There is no CUDA allocator OOM during model loading.
A serving workload is healthy at 2K context but reaches KV cache capacity at 8K context with the same number of users.
vLLM is given /models/qwen but config.json is actually under /models/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, so it reports that the local path is not a valid model.
The configured local directory exists but contains only a README and no config.json or safetensors files.
A relative model path resolves from the wrong working directory and vLLM cannot find tokenizer.json in that location.
The service points at a parent cache directory instead of the pinned snapshot directory containing config.json and model shards.
Startup says the supplied path is missing configuration files; network access is intentionally disabled because the model should be local.
An unbounded burst sends hundreds of requests to a healthy service; queue time and P95 TTFT explode while each completed request is correct.
Latency SLO failures occur only when arrival rate exceeds sustainable throughput. GPU memory and model artifacts remain stable.
The API accepts every request during a traffic spike, causing a long queue and timeouts without engine crashes.
A load test with unlimited concurrency drives goodput toward zero because most requests miss TTFT SLO despite nonzero raw throughput.
The service is fast at controlled concurrency but degrades sharply when the gateway removes its request limit and admits a large burst.
The selected FP8 kernel reports that the GPU architecture does not support the requested precision mode, while BF16 starts successfully.
Starting with an experimental cache dtype fails an architecture capability check before any requests arrive; using bfloat16 avoids the failure.
A quantized attention backend requires a newer compute capability than the installed GPU and rejects initialization.
The engine can load model weights in BF16 but raises not implemented when KV cache dtype is changed to an unsupported low-precision format.
A low-precision execution path is unavailable for this device generation, and the same configuration works after selecting a supported dtype.
The benchmark tokenizes prompts with a newer tokenizer revision than the server model snapshot, producing different token IDs for the same text.
Requests fail alignment checks because the client uses a tokenizer from another Qwen model while the server uses Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct.
Prompt lengths measured by the benchmark disagree with server usage after only tokenizer files were updated in the local snapshot.
Special chat tokens are encoded as ordinary text because the client tokenizer revision does not match the pinned model revision.
The server is offline-capable, but the benchmark silently downloads a different tokenizer and reports input lengths unlike the controlled run.
